paras.t: Self-catering apartments with sea views, just two minutes from the beach. Each apartment has a fully equipped kitchen and a balcony. Minimum stay three nights. Sorry, no pets. Free parking for one car per apartment.

A peaceful guesthouse in the countryside, ten kilometres from town. A full cooked breakfast is included in the price, and evening meals made with vegetables from our own garden are available on request. Well-behaved dogs welcome. Ideal for walkers.

Tent pitches and caravans to rent, a short walk from the town centre. Shower block, laundry and a small shop selling basic food. The cheapest option in the area, especially for families. Open April to September only.
Our historic hotel in the town centre offers luxury rooms, a heated indoor pool and a restaurant that has won national awards. Guests can borrow bicycles free of charge to explore the coast.

Shared and private rooms for travellers on a budget. Guests can use the shared kitchen to prepare their own meals. Open all year. Lockers are provided, but please bring your own padlock. Organised walking tours every Saturday.

passages.title: City Buses: lost property
paras: City Buses operates a lost property service for items found on our buses. When a driver finds an item, it is kept on the bus until the end of the day and then taken to the depot where the bus is based.

Items are kept at the depot for two days. After that, they are sent to our central Lost Property Office at Victoria Bus Station, where they are stored for one month. Items that are not collected within that time are given to charity, except for documents such as passports, which are returned to the relevant authorities.

If you have lost something, please complete the online form on our website, giving as much detail as possible, including the route number and the approximate time of your journey. You can also report a lost item by telephone, but please note that our phone line is very busy, especially on Monday mornings, so the online form is usually quicker.

We will contact you if an item matching your description is found. To collect an item, you will need to bring photo identification. If you are unable to collect it yourself, another person may do so on your behalf, provided they bring a signed letter from you as well as their own identification.

A small charge of £3 is made for each item collected, to cover our handling costs. There is no charge for wallets, purses or keys, or for items belonging to children under sixteen. Unfortunately, for reasons of hygiene, we cannot keep food, drinks or items of clothing that are wet or dirty. Mobile phones are kept, but staff are not permitted to switch them on or answer them.

passages.title: Greenfield Kitchen: safety rules for new staff
paras: Welcome to the team at Greenfield Kitchen. Before you start your first shift, please read the following safety rules carefully. If anything is unclear, ask the head chef, who is responsible for health and safety in the kitchen.

Personal hygiene is essential. Wash your hands thoroughly when you arrive, after every break and whenever you move from handling raw meat to other foods. Long hair must be tied back and covered with a hat. You may wear a plain wedding ring, but all other jewellery, including watches, must be removed before you enter the kitchen.

Our kitchen uses a colour-coded system for chopping boards to prevent food contamination. Red boards are for raw meat, blue for fish, and green for fruit and vegetables. Boards must be cleaned in the dishwasher after use, not simply rinsed under the tap.

Accidents are most often caused by slippery floors. Any spill should be cleaned up immediately, and a yellow warning sign placed on the wet area until it is completely dry. Staff must wear the non-slip shoes provided by the company at all times in the kitchen.

Knives should always be carried with the point facing downwards, and never left in the sink, where someone may reach in without seeing them. If you cut yourself, however small the injury, you must use a blue plaster from the first aid box, so that it can easily be seen if it falls into food, and record the incident in the accident book, which is kept in the manager’s office.
Finally, all new staff are required to complete a short online food safety course within their first two weeks. The company pays for the course, and staff are paid for the time they spend on it.

passages.title: Staff parking permits
paras: Staff who wish to park in the company car park must hold a valid parking permit. Because the number of spaces is limited, permits are not given automatically, and priority is given to staff who would find it difficult to travel to work by other means.

To apply, complete the parking permit form, which is available from the facilities team on the ground floor. You will need to provide the registration number of your vehicle and a copy of your driving licence. Applications are considered once a month, and you will be told the result within ten working days of the monthly deadline.

Permits are valid for twelve months and cost £10 per month, which is taken directly from your salary. Staff who share a car with at least one colleague receive their permit free of charge, and a number of spaces near the main entrance are reserved for car sharers.

If you change your vehicle, you must inform the facilities team so that your permit can be updated. Permits cannot be transferred to other members of staff. Vehicles parked without a permit, or in spaces reserved for visitors, may receive a warning notice; after three warnings, the permit holder may lose the right to park on site.

The company also supports other ways of travelling to work. A secure bicycle shelter is located beside the staff entrance, and showers are available on the first floor. Staff can also join our scheme for buying a bicycle, which allows the cost to be spread over twelve months.

passages.title: The bicycle: a machine that changed society
paras: It is easy to forget how revolutionary the bicycle once was. Before it appeared, ordinary people who could not afford a horse had only one way of travelling over land: on foot. The bicycle gave them, for the first time, a cheap and independent means of covering long distances, and in doing so it changed society in ways its inventors could never have imagined.

The first machine that could be described as a bicycle was built in 1817 by a German inventor, Karl von Drais. It had two wheels and a seat, but no pedals; the rider pushed it along by running with his feet on the ground. Von Drais hoped it would replace horses, which were in short supply after a series of poor harvests had left little food for animals. His ‘running machine’ was briefly fashionable among wealthy young men, but it was heavy and uncomfortable, and the fashion soon passed.

In the 1860s, French makers added pedals to the front wheel. The new machines were nicknamed ‘boneshakers’, because their wooden wheels and iron tyres made riding on the rough roads of the time extremely uncomfortable. Because the pedals were fixed directly to the wheel, the only way to go faster was to make the wheel bigger. This led to the high-wheeler, or ‘penny-farthing’, whose front wheel could be as tall as a man. It was fast, but it was also dangerous: riders sat so high that a small stone could throw them over the handlebars, and it was used almost entirely by athletic young men.

The breakthrough came in 1885 with the ‘safety bicycle’, designed by the Englishman John Kemp Starley. It had two wheels of equal size and a chain that connected the pedals to the back wheel. Riders could now go fast without sitting high above the ground. Soon afterwards, the invention of the air-filled rubber tyre by John Dunlop, originally to make his son’s tricycle more comfortable, made riding far smoother. The basic design of Starley’s machine has hardly changed since.

What followed was a cycling craze. In the 1890s, millions of bicycles were sold in Europe and North America. For working people, the bicycle meant that they could live further from their workplace, and some historians have even suggested that it widened the choice of marriage partners in rural areas, as young people could now easily visit neighbouring villages.

The bicycle had a particularly important effect on the lives of women. Cycling was impossible in the long, heavy skirts that were fashionable at the time, and many women adopted shorter skirts or loose trousers called ‘bloomers’. This shocked many people, but it also gave women a new freedom of movement. The American campaigner Susan B. Anthony said in 1896 that the bicycle had done more to free women than anything else in the world.

Cyclists also changed the landscape. In Britain and the United States, cycling clubs campaigned for smoother roads, and their efforts led to improvements that later benefited motorists. Ironically, the rise of the motor car in the twentieth century pushed bicycles off many roads. Today, however, concerns about pollution and health have led to a revival, and many cities are building cycle lanes once again.
